extracted.intended_audience: general readers, fans, and researchers interested in Tina Fey and comic performance/style
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and characterize the qualities, techniques, and professional choices that define Tina Fey's comedic and acting style (as described in a biographical/wiki article). Useful for analyzing or emulating a contemporary TV/sketch comedian's persona and approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadpan humor and delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Fey is known for her deadpan humor and delivery; her 'sardonic wit' has become a professional trademark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics comment on how her delivery projects 'both oblivious security and hyper-alert insecurity' and that her deadpan delivery is a defining performance trait across roles. Examples: critics repeatedly note this as central to her comic persona.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sardonic wit / clear comic voice
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'sardonic wit' and a 'very clear take on things' — an identifiable, intelligent, edged voice that audiences recognize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lorne Michaels: 'It always comes from a place of intelligence and there is just an edge to it.' Michaels adds it's 'not fearful. It's strong and confident and you recognise the voice.' Use of a consistent, recognizable viewpoint is presented as a marker of quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-deprecating humor (using herself as butt of jokes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Seldom hesitating to use herself as the butt of her own jokes; practices self-deprecating humor extensively (e.g., Liz Lemon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page discusses both praise (makes her relatable; gives permission to be imperfect) and criticism (may reinforce negative ideas about women's appearance). Guidance: self-deprecation can be an 'art' that connects with audiences but may be interpreted differently depending on context and audience; examples and debate included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between comedy and cruelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to 'strike a balance between comedy and cruelty' — particularly noted in her Sarah Palin impersonation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entertainment Weekly praised the Palin impersonation for balancing comedic bite without gratuitous nastiness; this balance is presented as a criterion for successful political satire/impersonation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situational, ironic, and character-driven comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Specializes in 'delectable, situational and ironic comedy' and writes/acts in material that is quirky and character-driven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Her scripts are described as 'carefully written' and 'quirky and character-driven' (30 Rock). This suggests emphasis on situation and character over mere gag-density; examples include 30 Rock's writing and structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of physical and improvisational techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Her acting is influenced by both physical and improvisational comedy practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While her scripts are carefully written, performance draws on improvisation and physicality—indicating a hybrid approach: prepared writing plus performative spontaneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persona construction (use of props/costume as identity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fey 'fashioned her comic persona around her glasses' — using visual elements as part of comic identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page recounts Fey joking that 'Glasses make anyone look smarter'; using a consistent visual cue can reinforce a recognisable persona in performance and publicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relatability via imperfect, anxious protagonist type
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequently portrays 'the hilarious, self-deprecating unmarried career woman' or an anxious overthinker; relatability is a core trait.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics note that this recurring type (e.g., Liz Lemon) allows audiences to connect; Fey also chooses roles by asking 'Would I be plausible in this role, in this job?,' indicating plausibility/relatability as selection criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate role selection and range awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberate about taking only parts suited to her range; realistic about her range as a leading lady.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Boston Globe and Fey herself note she is 'deliberate about only taking on parts for which she actually seems suited.' This is presented as a professional standard for role choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to push boundaries / write borderline jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Has garnered criticism for being politically incorrect but defends writing 'borderline jokes' and has 'opted out' of the culture demanding apologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This suggests a criterion where risk-taking and boundary-pushing are valued by Fey (and some critics) as part of comedic authenticity; also alerts to potential backlash and the need for considered intent/context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of whining in self-deprecating material
rubrics_metrics.description: Her material 'lacks "whining"' — self-deprecation without plaintive or victimizing tones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page contrasts Fey's self-deprecation with older styles where performers used themselves as punching bags; the modern effective approach is self-deprecating but assertive, not plaintive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parodic use of self to critique media/culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Uses self-deprecation and parody 'to show up our culture' — mocking cultural obsessions (e.g., appearance) rather than endorsing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics argue Fey's mockery of her appearance is intended to parody media that values looks above ability; effective comedic critique can reframe cultural norms rather than reinforce them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scriptwriting craft: careful, quirky, character-driven scripts
rubrics_metrics.description: As a writer, Fey's scripts are described as 'carefully written' and often 'quirky and character-driven.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This entry emphasizes craftsmanship in writing (structure, character work) as a standard for quality in sitcom/satirical writing—30 Rock cited as exemplar; suggests prioritizing strong character arcs and voice.
